# From Chinese characters to Unicode: the journey of Māzǔ

Long before it was a domain, this name traveled through scripts. **Māzǔ** begins in Chinese characters, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that journey preserves some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its spelling.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Māzǔ
- **ASCII form:** mazu
- **Meaning:** "Mother ancestor"
- **Domain of influence:** Sea, Protection, Seafaring
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 媽祖 (Chinese characters)
- **Live domain:** māzǔ.com

## Overview

**Māzǔ** (*mazu*) — Sea, Protection, Seafaring · Mother ancestor — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sea, Protection, Seafaring". The name means "Mother ancestor".

Māzǔ is the most-worshipped sea goddess on earth: the fisherman's daughter who became the guardian of everyone who works the water, whose temples line every coast of the Chinese world, and whose red lanterns guide sailors home through a thousand years of storms.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Māzǔ** and serves its temple at [māzǔ.com](https://xn--mz-dla95f.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *mazu* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Chinese characters as **媽祖**. Etymologically it means "Mother ancestor".

The ASCII form *mazu* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Māzǔ** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **ā** — Long vowel
- **z** → **z** — Same
- **u** → **ǔ** — Special character

The project holds the domain **māzǔ.com** (xn--mz-dla95f.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Chinese characters as **媽祖**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *mazu* and the PuniCodex restoration **Māzǔ** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/má.tsù/** — Standard Mandarin.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: MAH-tsoo — level tone, then a dip-and-rise.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 媽祖
- **Her title** — Tiānhòu (天后)
- **Cantonese** — Tin Hau
- **Owned form** — Māzǔ

Māzǔ 媽祖 — "Maternal Ancestor" — carries the first tone on mā and the dipping third tone on zǔ; the restoration keeps both tone marks. Her personal name was Lín Mòniáng ("Silent Maiden"), but the world prays to the title: Grandmother of the sea. The third tone on zǔ dips and rises — the small valley in the name that Mandarin speakers sing without noticing.

## Mythology

Māzǔ's myth is a life, not a legend: the historical Lín Mòniáng of 10th-century Meizhou, whose silence, visions, and early death became the sea's own religion.

### The Silent Girl of Meizhou (The Maiden)

Lín Mòniáng was born on Meizhou island in 960 CE, and tradition says she did not cry at birth — hence "Silent Maiden." She learned to read the weather on her father's fishing boat, stood on the shore watching for lost sails, and was seen in dreams guiding drowning sailors home. Dead by twenty-eight, she rose, the fishermen said, straight to the sky on a cloud of incense — and the sea was never without her again.

### From Daughter to Empress of Heaven (The Apotheosis)

The dynasties out-titled each other: the Song made her Consort of Heaven, the Yuan made her Princess, the Ming made her Holy Mother, the Qing made her Tiānhòu — Empress of Heaven. The historical woman is buried in the titles: the fishing daughter became, by twelve centuries of gratitude, the highest-ranked goddess of the Chinese sea, outranking every god the bureaucracy could promote her past.

### Eyes and Ears of the Sea (The Generals)

Her two attendants are the myth of vigilance itself: Qiānlǐyǎn ("thousand-mile eye") and Shùnfēng'ěr ("with-the-wind ear"), the demon-generals she tamed to watch and listen for sailors in distress. Their horned, fierce statues flank her in every temple — the goddess's instruments: nothing that happens on her sea goes unseen or unheard.

### The Island Procession (The Pilgrimage)

Her living myth is the Dajia Māzú pilgrimage: each year her statue walks 340 kilometers around Taiwan for nine days, and a million people walk with it — touch the palanquin, kneel as it passes, weep when it returns home. The largest annual religious procession in the Chinese world is not to a cathedral but after a fisherman's daughter, walking the roads she still guards.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Māzǔ concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The red robe** — Her temple color — protection worn bright against the grey sea
- **The lantern** — The guide-light of the storm-tossed
- **The two generals** — Sight and hearing deified — vigilance in both directions

## Archaeology & Evidence

The Meizhou Ancestral Temple on her home island — rebuilt repeatedly from the Song original, crowded with imperial plaques — is her Nazareth; the Dajia Jenn Lann Temple and Taipei's grand Tianhou temples are her living capitals. Macau's A-Ma Temple (15th c., older than the Portuguese) marks her oldest colonial-era shore, and the Mazu statues of the Taiwan Strait's temples document eight centuries of her iconography.

## Realm & Domain

Māzǔ is the most-worshipped sea goddess on earth: the fisherman's daughter who became the guardian of everyone who works the water, whose temples line every coast of the Chinese world, and whose red lanterns guide sailors home through a thousand years of storms.

### The Sailors' Guardian

The goddess of everyone who goes to sea — the busiest answering voice on the water.

### The Red Lantern

Her signal in the storm — the light sailors pray to see.

### The Two Generals

Qiānlǐyǎn and Shùnfēng'ěr — her thousand-mile eyes and wind-sharp ears.

### Meizhou

Her island home off Fujian — the Nazareth of the sea-faith.

## Across Cultures

She absorbs the coast's other sea-powers: associated with Guānyīn (who is sometimes her patron in the legends), honored in Daoist and Buddhist temples alike, and worshipped as Tin Hau in Hong Kong and A-Ma in Macau — whose very name, some say, comes from her ("A-Ma-Gau," Bay of A-Ma). The diaspora carried her to every Chinese port from San Francisco to Sydney: wherever junks and container ships anchor, her shrine overlooks the harbor.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[aseratu|Ašeratu]], [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[ea|Ēa]], [[manannan|Manannán]], [[njordr|Njǫrðr]], and [[pontos|Póntos]], each linked through sea / water.

## Cultural Legacy

Her temples number in the thousands — over 1,500 in Taiwan alone; her birthday (23rd of the 3rd lunar month) shuts down the island's coasts; her Dajia procession is a national institution watched by millions more online. Fishermen, sailors, the navy, and migrants all claim her: the goddess who was once a girl watching the sea is now the sea's own government, elected annually by the crowds who walk behind her statue.

## A Meditation

Māzǔ is the goddess of being watched for. Not of the sea — of the people on it: the daughter who never stopped standing on the shore. She asks the question every sailor, parent, and lighthouse-keeper knows: who is watching the water for you — and for whom, tonight, are you the lantern?

Watch the procession and you see the whole theology: no priest lectures, no scripture is read — the statue simply walks, and a million people walk after it. The sea-faith never needed a doctrine; it needed a mother on the shore. Every year she makes the circuit, and every year the coast remembers that someone is watching the water.

The two generals at her flanks are the liturgy in one image: see far, hear far. Everything else — the titles, the temples, the processions — is commentary.

Her sea is the busiest water in human history — the straits that carried tea, silk, migrants, and war — and her temples face it still, unmoved by cargo schedules. The junks are gone; the lantern remains. Every container ship passing the Taiwan Strait sails through the parish of a fisherman's daughter, whether it knows it or not.

She is proof that the largest religions are made of gratitude, not doctrine. Nobody was ever converted to Māzǔ. They were simply rescued, and remembered.

The generals' statues unsettle children and reassure sailors: ugliness conscripted into vigilance, the demons made watchmen. It is the sea's whole covenant in two figures — the dangers are not banished but put on guard duty. Her temples teach it without a single sermon: what you cannot calm, you can still set to watching.

Her economy is miracles per capita, and her ledger is full: every coastal family keeps one — the grandfather guided home, the net that held, the storm that turned. Gratitude at that scale stops being sentiment and becomes infrastructure, the sea's own safety service, funded by incense, staffed by a daughter of Fujian, open every hour of every storm.

## The Unicode Restoration

Māzǔ is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *mazu* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 4 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 1 mark of length (ā); 1 further adjustment (ǔ). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Character by Character

The journey from *mazu* to **Māzǔ**, one character at a time:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **ā** — Long vowel
- **z** → **z** — Same
- **u** → **ǔ** — Special character

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **māzǔ.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--mz-dla95f.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Māzǔ; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Chinese characters can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Māzǔ mean?** The traditional gloss is "Mother ancestor."

**Which tradition does Māzǔ belong to?** Māzǔ is catalogued in the Chinese pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**Why is Māzǔ classified as Tier 1?** Because the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses — and the marks in the restored spelling preserve exactly that evidence.

**Is Māzǔ a working domain?** Yes — māzǔ.com resolves today and routes to this temple.

**What is the punycode for māzǔ.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--mz-dla95f.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Māzǔ in a normal browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts mazu to Māzǔ for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Every stage of the journey from Chinese characters to Unicode was an act of care: the scribe who first wrote the name, the lexicographer who glossed it, the engineer who taught the DNS to carry it. The PuniCodex restoration is the latest stage, not the last word — the Scholarly Edition is revised as the evidence improves. What does not change is the principle: a name deserves to be written the way its own tradition wrote it. **Māzǔ** in the address bar is that principle, made routable.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Māzǔ**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *mazu* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 4 characters, 2 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **m** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **a** becomes **ā** — Long vowel.

The **z** stays as it is — Same.

The **u** becomes **ǔ** — Special character.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

## Māzǔ in Its Tradition

**Māzǔ** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is counted among 59 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Sea, Protection, Seafaring — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Māzǔ**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Māzǔ** is one such vote.
